II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01980

“I was dismayed by the length of that wait. I spent the first forty days among them, waiting and praying to God night and day to hasten the ships' arrival. Throughout that time everyone treated me with the greatest kindness, regard and consideration. At the end of the fortieth day, my heart grew anxious, because the waiting seemed as though it would never end. I went out and walked along the seashore, searching the open water toward the west, for the inhabitants had assured me that it was from that direction their provisions arrived.” Remembering the route followed thus far, we may be inclined to imagine ourselves on the Atlantic coast of Africa, with the island perhaps belonging to the Canary Islands.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01981

But we would be mistaken. We have already begun to suspect this, and everything that follows will confirm it—beginning with the length of the sea voyage still before us. The topography, however precisely described, no longer belongs to the kind of geography we can recover from our maps. Elsewhere, indeed, traditions “locate” this Green Island, which here appears almost as a surviving fragment of Atlantis, in quite different places—the Caspian Sea, for example. Which is another way of saying that it has no coordinates in the geography of this world.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01982

Our traveller stood watching on the shore, like a lookout. “Suddenly,” he says, “one day I saw something white moving far away. I questioned the local people. ‘Isn't that a white bird out there on the sea? — No,’ they said. ‘Can you see something? — Yes,’ I answered. Then they burst into joy. ‘Those,’ they told me, ‘are the ships that come to us every year from the land of the Imam's sons.’”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01983

“Only a short time passed before the ships came into view. According to the inhabitants, they had arrived earlier than usual. A great ship entered the harbour, followed by another, then another, until the whole fleet of seven ships had arrived.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01984

“From the great ship there descended a shaykh of noble bearing, handsome and splendidly dressed. He went straight to the mosque, performed his ablutions and the two afternoon prayers according to the rites handed down to us from the holy Imams—that is, in the Shiite manner. When he had finished, he turned to me and greeted me. I returned his greeting.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01985

“‘What is your name?’ he asked. ‘I believe your name is 'Ali? — You are right,’ I replied. He then spoke with me as someone might who had known me very well for a long time. ‘And what is your father's name?’ he asked. ‘Fazel, I believe. Is that not so? — Yes,’ I said. After that I no longer doubted that he must have travelled with our party, in our caravan, from Damascus to Cairo.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01986
“‘Shaykh,’ I asked him, ‘how do you know my father and me? Were you with us when we travelled from Damascus to Cairo?
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01987
“— Certainly not.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01988
“— And you were not with us on our journey from Cairo to Andalusia either?
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01989
“— No! I swear by my lord, the Imam of this age, that I was not with you.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01990
“— Then how do you know my name, and how do you know my father's name?
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01991

“— Know that, long before today, a description of you reached me, together with knowledge of your name, your origin, your appearance and your father's name—may God receive him in His mercy! For you must understand: I am your Companion. I have come to take you with me to the Green Island. We shall set out together for the Green Island now.’”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01992

In this episode we unmistakably recognize the feeling known to seekers of hidden spiritual knowledge in every age and place: the feeling of exile. Such a person is cut off from his own people, from a family of good and beautiful beings whom he can barely remember, and whose way home he knows even less. Then one day a message comes from them—like the letter in the Hymn of the Pearl, in the Acts of Thomas, reminding the young Parthian prince of his origin; or like the message brought by the hoopoe to the exile imprisoned at the bottom of a well in Suhrawardi's Tale of the Western Exile. Here we have something more than a message.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01993

One of those beings comes in person: one of the mysterious Companions of the Hidden Imam, appointed to accompany the man he has been sent to bring “home.” Our narrator then cries out with great feeling: “When I heard these words, I was beside myself with happiness. So they had remembered me! So they knew my name!” Was his exile, then, at an end?
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01994

The shaykh, whose name was simply Muhammad, stayed only three days—long enough to make sure that all the provisions intended for each of the Shiites on the peninsula had been distributed. Then they decided to depart. They boarded the great ship, the signal was given, and they sailed out to sea.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01995

“On the sixteenth day of our voyage,” continues 'Ali ibn Fazel's account—and we should note this precision, since from here onward it is the only detail that gives us a sense of distance actually travelled—“I noticed that the water on the surface of the sea was completely white. Shaykh Muhammad came over to me. ‘I see,’ he said, ‘that this water has particularly caught your attention.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01996
“— Because,” I told him, “I've noticed that it is a different colour from the rest of the sea.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01997

“— Indeed,” he said. “This water is the White Sea, and there on the horizon is the Green Island. This white water forms a circle all around the island, like a fortified wall protecting a city. From whatever direction one approaches, one must pass through it. And by the wisdom of the Absolute Wise One, and through the spiritual power flowing from our lord and Imam who reigns over this age, whenever the ships of our enemies enter these waters, they sink, however strong and powerful they may be.”’” (This detail assures us that we have now entered the geography of another world.)
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01998
The narrator admits that he wanted to taste this water for himself. He drew up a little of it. “It tasted,” he says, “just like the water of the Euphrates.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-01999

“When we had crossed this belt of white water, we finally landed on the Green Island, whose inhabitants live in a state of perpetual youth. We disembarked from the great ship, set foot on the island, and entered the city. I saw that the city stood beside the sea and had ramparts and towers; seven walls encircled it. There were plentiful rivers and luxuriant vegetation, with every kind of fruit tree. There were shops and many public bathhouses (hammam). Most of the buildings were made of translucent marble. All the inhabitants wore magnificent clothing. Their faces were beautiful. My heart soared with joy at everything I beheld.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02000

Here begins the second part of the initiation story. We can distinguish three stages. First comes a series of conversations with the man who governs the Green Island and is none other than a grandson of the Hidden Imam. These conversations offer a first initiation into the Imam's secret. Then comes a visit to a mysterious sanctuary deep within the mountain that rises above the island. Finally, there is another series of conversations, of decisive importance.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02001

After the travellers had rested, Shaykh Muhammad took his companion to the Great Mosque. There he saw a large assembly, “at the centre of which,” says the narrator, “sat a man whose majesty and dignity, gentleness and serenity, were beyond my power to describe.” People addressed him as Sayyed Shamsoddin Muhammad al-'Alim, meaning “the learned man,” or “the sage.” Sayyed Shamsoddin was presiding over something like what we today would call a close reading of texts. One person after another would read aloud to him a passage from the Qur'an or from the sources of Imami theology—that is, the hadith, the transmitted sayings of the Imams—and he would comment on their interpretations, correct them, and fill out what was missing.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02002

'Ali ibn Fazel was introduced, and the Sayyed graciously seated him beside himself. He asked about his journey and then said these significant words: “Everything concerning you came to my knowledge long before today. It was on my instructions that your companion, Shaykh Muhammad, brought you here.” Our traveller then withdrew to a room in one of the mosque's annexes, which had been set aside for him, and rested until late afternoon.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02003

As evening fell, “the one to whose care I had been entrusted,” as he calls Shaykh Muhammad, his companion in initiation—using almost exactly the expression we find in The Shepherd of Hermas—“told me that the Sayyed and his companions would come to share our evening meal.” And so they did. When the meal was finished, everyone rose and went to the mosque to recite the evening prayer, after which each returned home.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02004

Three weeks—or eighteen days, to be exact—passed in long conversations, at the end of which our pilgrim received his first revelation. The first time he joined his new companions for the solemn Friday prayer, he noticed that the Sayyed doubled the deep bows (rak'at) each time, treating them as obligatory.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02005

Yet according to the Shiite rite, this obligation applies only when the Imam is present. 'Ali ibn Fazel thought to himself, “So there are times when the Imam is here?” At the first opportunity to speak to the Sayyed alone, he asked him: “Is the Imam present here? — No,” answered the Sayyed, “but I am his personal representative (na'ib khass), by an order that comes directly from him. — My lord,” I said, “have you seen the Imam? — No. But my father told me that he had heard the Imam's voice without seeing him, whereas my grandfather both heard his voice and saw him in person.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02006

Two valuable points emerge here. First, we are certainly no longer in a place belonging to this world, where no one could claim to be the Hidden Imam's “representative,” still less to be descended from him—as will be explained later.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02007

Second, there is something here that recalls the Shiite understanding of spiritual knowledge. To hear the voice without seeing the one who inspires is the characteristic form of the Imam's inward inspiration (ilham); to hear the words and at the same time see the Angel is characteristic of the divine revelation (wahy) received by the prophets.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02008

But another question now becomes urgent—so urgent that it will be asked again at the end of the story. “And why, my lord, is this privilege given to one person and withheld from another? Why does one man see him, while another does not?” The answer will allude to the deepest secret of Twelver Shiism, and at the same time to the secret of the Green Island.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02009

“Brother,” the Sayyed told me, “God bestows His grace upon whichever of His faithful servants He wills, in accordance with His perfect wisdom and sovereign majesty. Among His servants God has set apart those He has chosen as prophets, messengers, and inheritors of the prophetic mission (awsiya', the Imams). He has established them as Signs and symbols (a'lam) for humankind, as Witnesses and Guides (Hojjat) before His creatures, as intermediaries between them and Himself.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02010

“Thus, only after the Sign has shone forth may ‘those who perish perish, and those who live live.’ For in His tender care God never leaves the Earth without a Witness and Guarantor who answers for Him before human beings. Yet it sometimes happens that a Witness himself needs an intermediary to convey to people, in his name, what he has to tell them.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02011

That is precisely the situation of the last of these Witnesses, the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. The profound conviction of Shiism, as we have already had occasion to say, is that human beings must never be able to argue against God that there was no Witness in the world to answer for Him. It is this very necessity that establishes the necessity of the Imamate after the prophetic mission has come to an end. And the Imamate continues even during the Imam's Occultation, because the ultimate reason for that concealment is to be sought entirely on the human side.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02012

In himself, the Imam remains the Imam, whether people recognize him or whether he is wholly unknown to the mass of humankind. He remains the Pole of poles, without whose existence the human world could not continue to exist: the mystical Pole (Qotb), at the summit of a spiritual hierarchy governed by the same sacred law of remaining incognito. For God alone chooses the human beings to whom one of the Imam's Companions—or sometimes the Imam himself—will appear.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02013

After this conversation, Sayyed Shamsoddin took 'Ali ibn Fazel by the hand—as Gurnemanz leads Parsifal toward the realm of the Grail—and they left the city together. “We walked toward the gardens. Streams of living water lay before us, and garden followed garden, with beautiful trees bearing every kind of delicious fruit ... I had never seen anything like it in either of the two Iraqs (Arab Iraq and Persian Iraq), or anywhere in Syria. As we were passing from one garden to another, we saw a handsome man coming toward us, dressed in two layers of white woollen cloth.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02014

“As he passed, he greeted us and went on his way. His appearance struck me. I asked the Sayyed, ‘Who is that man? — Do you see that high mountain?’ the Sayyed asked me. ‘— Yes,’ I said. ‘— Well, deep within that mountain is a beautiful place where a spring of living water flows beneath a tree—a very great tree, with branches spreading in every direction. Beside the spring stands a domed place of prayer (qobba), built of brick. That man and a companion of his are the guardians of this little sanctuary.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02015

“I myself go there every Friday morning to make my visit to the Imam. I perform a prayer of two cycles (rak'at), and there I find a sheet of paper on which are written the decisions to be made concerning the believers. Everything written there I put into practice. You too should go there and pay your visit to the Imam in that sanctuary.’”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02016

For our part, we seem to recognize in passing, in the man dressed in white wool, the mysterious Khezr (Khadir), the counterpart of the prophet Elijah, sometimes identified with him, who has a special bond with the Twelfth Imam. (At Jam-Karan, in the preceding story, we encountered him reading aloud in the Imam's presence). What confirms this identification for us is his presence here beside a spring that can only be the Spring of Life. It flows in the shade of a great tree, the Tuba tree, which spreads its shadow over paradise and is the Tree of Being. And so it is there, at the very heart of being, beneath the Tree and beside the Spring, that we find the sanctuary where one may draw nearest to the Hidden Imam.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02017

“So I made my way toward the mountain,” our pilgrim continues. “I found the domed place of prayer exactly where the Sayyed had said it would be, and just as he had described it. I also found its two guardians. The one we had met in the gardens welcomed me, while the other gave me a cold look. The first said to him, ‘Do not be unfriendly, for I saw him in the company of Sayyed Shamsoddin al-'Alim.’ At this the second man turned to me and welcomed me too.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02018

“Both began talking with me and then offered me bread and grapes—not the bread and wine of the mystical Last Supper, since we are in Islam, but the same symbols: bread and grapes. I drank the Water flowing beside the sanctuary, performed my ritual ablutions, and offered a prayer of two cycles. Then I ventured to ask the guardians whether it was possible to see the Imam. They said, ‘No, it is not possible to see him, and we are not permitted to tell anyone about this.’ So I asked them to pray for me. They both prayed for me, and then we parted.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02019

Returning from this pilgrimage, which seems to mark the high point of his stay on the Green Island, 'Ali ibn Fazel went to see his friend Shaykh Muhammad, who had come to fetch him and with whom he had sailed to the island. He told him everything about that memorable day: his ascent of the mountain, his meeting with the two guardians, and the unfriendly reception he had at first received from one of them. The shaykh explained: “If he acted that way at first, it was because he did not know you. For no one except Sayyed Shamsoddin and those who are like him is permitted to ascend to those places.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02020

But if the Sayyed had instructed 'Ali ibn Fazel to go up there, we must ask, did that mean that he had become one of those “like him”? There is surely a profound insight here into the meaning of Shiite devotion, one that a thinker such as Molla Sadra Shirazi was able to bring out so admirably. There is no opposition or contradiction between prophetic religion as a religion received from outside oneself and mystical religion as a religion experienced inwardly. When a spiritual seeker reaches the level at which the Imam becomes a personal, inward Guide, the seeker attains a state “like” that of the Imam. Far from abolishing the teachings concerning prophecy and the Imams, this experience fulfils them, makes them “real”.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02021

As for Sayyed Shamsoddin, the shaykh explained to his friend that he was a descendant, “one of the children of the Imam's children. Five fathers stand between him and the Imam”—that is, five generations. For anyone who insists on the material evidence of what are called historical facts, this is something extraordinary indeed. The Sayyed is a descendant of an Imam, an Imam-zadeh. He has a precise genealogy and a definite way of life; his teaching has real effects on human souls.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02022

And yet, even less than his forefather the Twelfth Imam, does he appear in the ordinary world of sensory experience. He is in no sense a “myth,” yet he does not enter “history.” Even what is called “docetism”—often without any real understanding of it—is surpassed by the boldness of this faith in the world beyond the senses, and by this world of vision, which is at once sacred knowledge (hierognosis) and sacred history (hierohistory).
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02023

We now come to the final part of the story. The initiation will be completed by clarifying one of the matters closest to every faithful Shiite's heart: the condition in which the Qur'an, the sacred Book sent down from Heaven, exists today. Then a scene of triumphant manifestation will lead naturally to a question about the Imam's future appearance. Once again, with the insistence of a theme that can never be forgotten, the question will arise: is it possible to see the Imam? This last conversation prepares the way for the farewell and the journey home.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02024

'Ali ibn Fazel, well trained in Qur'anic studies, knew the variant readings of the Qur'an perfectly and wanted the Sayyed's help in resolving the difficulties they presented. To test him, the Sayyed asked him to begin reciting the Qur'an. At every passage where variants occurred, the young Iranian listed all the readings preserved by those known in Persian as the haft pir, the seven masters of Qur'anic recitation.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02025

But the Sayyed interrupted him. We do not need all those authorities. What actually happened was this: during the Prophet's last pilgrimage, known as the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Angel Gabriel descended to him once more and had him recite the entire Qur'an. Gabriel reminded him of the circumstances in which its successive passages had been revealed, explained the variant readings, and gave particular attention to the concluding sections and final verses of each sura.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02026

Present were not only a group of well-known Companions but also the First Imam, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Commander of the Faithful, together with his two sons, Hasan and Hosayn. As the Angel spoke, 'Ali wrote down his explanations on a scroll of skin. Here, then, the Angel who interprets the text is none other than the Angel who revealed it.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02027
But why, 'Ali ibn Fazel asks, does the text seem so disjointed? Why do certain verses appear to have no connection with what comes before or after them?
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02028
The answer given is that, immediately after the Prophet's death, the First Imam tried to present to the Quraysh the complete Qur'an as he himself had written it down.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02029

But those who had seized the outward caliphate—for the real, hidden caliphate of the spirit was beyond their reach—rejected the Imam's offer with contempt. These were the first two caliphs recognized by the Sunnis, Abu Bakr and 'Omar, who thus set Islam on the course it subsequently followed. Instead they chose to gather, fragment by fragment, whatever portions of the text were in the possession of the Muslims. Naturally, they removed everything that clearly concerned the Imamate and might have testified against them. This, the account explains, is why the text has gaps and seems disjointed. In spite of them, however, the Book is indeed the Word of God.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02030
But the only authentic copy of its heavenly archetype—the copy written by the First Imam's own hand—is held by the one who is now the Hidden Imam.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02031

We can imagine that, once the conversation had taken this direction, it hardly remained confined to harmless questions of religious law. It must have touched on Shiite spiritual knowledge, but the rule of secrecy will prevent us from ever knowing what was said. 'Ali ibn Fazel himself warns us: “From the Sayyed's teaching I have written down the answers to a great many questions, about ninety in all. I possess the text. I have gathered them in a book that I have called The Teachings of Shams (al-fawa'id al-shamsiya).
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02032
“But I can make it known only to a select few among the faithful. You will see this book, God willing.” Alas, no one has yet reported finding a manuscript of it.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02033

Meanwhile, on the very next Friday, which fell on the middle day of the month—we have already encountered the symbolism of this date—the Sayyed had, as usual, led the prayers and begun presiding over his gathering of students when 'Ali ibn Fazel suddenly heard a great commotion outside the mosque. He asked what was happening. The Sayyed told him: “Whenever the middle day of the month falls on a Friday, the commanders of our army assemble to await the Joy”—the traditional expression, as we already know, for the Imam's manifestation.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02034

'Ali ibn Fazel asked permission to see them and went outside. There he found an assembly of horsemen, singing a triumphant hymn that called upon God to hasten the joy of the Appearance of the Imam who will bring the divine Cause to triumph, Muhammad al-Mahdi, who reigns invisibly over this age. How many knights make up this supernatural company? Three hundred and thirteen, the Sayyed later explained. This is indeed one of the numbers given by traditions concerning the hidden spiritual hierarchy, always present incognito in this world in the Imam's service.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02035
But here, as the account specifies, the number refers only to the commanders of this esoteric army.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02036

This moving scene naturally led 'Ali ibn Fazel to ask the question every Shiite carries deep in the heart: “When will the Joy—the future appearance of the Imam—take place? — Brother,” the Sayyed answered, “that knowledge belongs to God alone, and the matter rests with His will, so completely that even the Imam himself does not know.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02037
“But there will be Signs and indications announcing his appearance.” Here the image of the Sword enters the story: the Sword will speak, asking the Imam to wield it.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02038

But this is a sword that has descended from Heaven, not a blade forged from the metals of this world. These two details suggest that the Imam's battles and victories will not be quite what some enthusiastic literal-minded believers perhaps expect. We also know that his manifestation cannot even be conceived until human beings have changed their hearts and become capable of seeing him.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02039

“To see the Imam.” This burning desire runs through the story from beginning to end. 'Ali ibn Fazel knew perfectly well the terms of the Imam's last letter, in which he had declared in advance that anyone claiming to have seen him would be an impostor. “How is it, then,” he asks, “that there are people among you who see him? — What you say is true,” replies the Sayyed. “The Imam did indeed make that declaration at the time, because his enemies were so numerous—alas, even among his own family, as well as elsewhere, among the pharaoh-like brood of the Abbasids. The need for secrecy was then so great that Shiites forbade themselves even to speak of the matter among themselves.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02040

“But much time has passed since then. Our enemies have abandoned all hope of reaching the Imam. This land of ours lies beyond their reach, beyond their power to do us violence. Through the spiritual influence of the Imam, none of our enemies is able to come as far as this place.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02041

The inviolable Green Island is therefore truly like the realm of the Grail, the land “on distant shores that no mortal can approach,” except those summoned by a mysterious message. Only they may be admitted for a time, and even they do not find the road through any initiative of their own. We already know that the Imam may appear to any human being in distress, but that the person will almost always understand who appeared only afterward. This very truth will be disclosed, through a kind of argument addressed to the traveller's own experience, in a farewell scene that must be translated in full: it cannot be summarized.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02042
“‘My lord,’ I said, ‘I would so love to stay among you until God permits the Joy’—that is, the Coming of the Imam.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02043

“‘Alas, my brother, even before today the order came to me that you must return to your own country, and neither you nor I can oppose that order. You have people dependent on you, and you have already been kept away from them for a very long time. You cannot delay any longer.’
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02044
“When I heard these words, I was overcome and wept. Then I said, ‘My lord, is there absolutely no possibility of changing the order that concerns me?’
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02045
“‘No. It is impossible.’
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02046
“‘Will you at least allow me to tell everything I have seen and heard here?’
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02047
“‘Nothing prevents you from telling the faithful believers, so that their hearts may be at peace. But you must tell it in a particular way.’”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02048
“And he told me what, in any event, I must not say (here again the ‘discipline of secrecy’ comes into play).
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02049
“‘My lord,’ I finally asked, ‘is it not possible to behold the beauty and radiance of the Imam?’
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02050
“‘No. But know this, my brother: a believer whose heart is wholly sincere may indeed see the Imam without knowing that it is the Imam he sees—without realizing it, without recognizing him.’
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02051
“‘But my lord, I am among those whose hearts are wholly sincere, and yet I have never seen the Imam!’
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02052

“‘On the contrary! You have seen him twice. The first time was when you were approaching Samarra, where you had never been before. Your companions had gone ahead, and you had fallen behind alone, having lost their trail. You came to a hollow in a dry riverbed. Just then you saw a young horseman riding toward you on a white horse, carrying a long lance tipped with Damascus steel. At first you were afraid he would take your clothes.

Nothing could suggest more powerfully than these last words of the Sayyed what Nâ-kojâ-Âbâd really is: the “place” that is not contained in any place in this world, yet can itself contain and encompass them all.

The story now hastens to its close. “Do not prolong your stay in the land of the West,” the Sayyed advises. The traveler is generously supplied with provisions for the journey. As money for the road, the Sayyed gives him gold coins whose inscriptions proclaim four things: the oneness of God (tawhîd), Mohammad’s prophetic mission, the Imamate of the First Imam, and that of the Twelfth.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

The ships are waiting—the very ships on which the traveler came to the Green Island, and which will now carry him away. He lands on the “Shiite peninsula,” where he had originally embarked with Shaykh Mohammad. From that point onward, however, our Iranian traveler covers his tracks. In accordance with Sayyed Shamsoddîn’s advice, he does not return to Andalusia.

We shall never know whether he was reunited with his beloved shaykh, who had been obliged to go and attend his aged father’s deathbed. The first identifiable city he mentions now is Tripoli, and only to tell us: “I joined the western pilgrimage caravan bound for Mecca. I performed the pilgrimage and then set out for Iraq, intending to settle in holy Najaf for the rest of my life.”

The Story of the Green Island invites a wealth of commentary. I have been able to draw attention to only a few of its recurring themes along the way; but even a brief survey shows how extraordinarily rich this story is.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02063

Let us single out those themes whose symbolic power gives the imaginative vision—this knowledge of sacred realities, or hierognosis—its remarkable coherence. 1) The Green Island is one of the islands belonging to the sons of the Twelfth Imam.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02064

We shall meet this theme again in another, shorter story. 2) Rather than depending on other lands for its sustenance, as an island of our world would be expected to do, the Green Island sustains other lands. It is a living symbol of the Source from which Shiite faith draws its nourishment. 3) It lies in the west. Here, therefore, the west does not particularly stand, as it does in Suhrawardi’s Tale of the Western Exile and throughout a whole realm of Gnostic thought, for the world of exile, the world of dark matter.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02065

The Green Island seems instead to correspond to what elsewhere is symbolized by Jâbarsâ, the city situated in the western region of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world. As a kind of “western paradise,” it bears a strange resemblance to Amitabha’s paradise in Pure Land Buddhism, or to Tir-nan-Og, “one of the otherworlds of the Celts,” the land of those who remain forever young.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02066

Moreover, since the Twelfth Imam himself invites comparison with Maitreya, the Buddha yet to come, we might also recall the mystical city of Shambhala. 4) Like the realm of the Grail, the Green Island is an intermediary world, directly connected with the higher worlds and complete in itself. 5) It is protected against every attempt to penetrate it from outside.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02067

Besides a stretch of sea that no enemy can cross, seven walls surround it and guard its approaches. (We are not told whether each wall is a different color, like those of ancient Ecbatana, present-day Hamadan, where Tobias and the Angel once came. An eleventh-century Ismaili author, Hamîdoddîn Kermânî, even organized one of his books, Râhat al-Aql, around the architecture of seven walls.) 6) No one can find the way there unless summoned. The person who is called receives a message, or a messenger, from the Invisible Ones, who know that person by name—or to whose family the person belongs. This is a characteristic feature of other Gnostic tales.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02068

7) A mountain rises above the Green Island. Deep within it, or at its summit, the Source of Life springs forth beneath the great symbolic Tree. There stands the small Temple where communication with the Hidden Imam is possible, tended by the mysterious prophet Khezr. 8) Like Montsalvat, the destination of the Grail quest, the inviolable Green Island is the place where believers draw near to the mystical Pole of the world: the Hidden Imam, who reigns invisibly over the present age and is the jewel of Shiite faith.

The account of the pilgrimage to the Green Island is not unique, though it may be the most characteristic example of this literature. At any rate, it is one document among many that testify to the intimate bond in which Shiite consciousness has lived with its Imam for more than ten centuries.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02070

One of the most striking features—also one of the most surprising when judged by the standards of rational consciousness—is the Hidden Imam’s family or descendants. (Here again we would have something like a dynasty of the Grail.) Yet none of his children or grandchildren succeeds him as Imam, since he himself remains the Imam throughout the period known as the Greater Occultation. The Green Island, as we have just seen, is one of the islands of the Imam’s sons.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02071

Another story, equally rich in detail, gives us a more precise account of their geography—though this, of course, is no geography we can transfer onto our maps. This story is more than a century and a half older than the Story of the Green Island, and we possess it only at second hand. Its compiler, a certain Mohammad ibn ‘Alî al-‘Alawî al-Hosaynî, based his text on the account of someone who heard the story directly, Kamâloddîn Ahmad ibn Mohammad al-Anbârî. Since this man reports the very words of the person who lived through the adventure, we again have a first-person narrative, a testimony.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02072

On the evening of 10 Ramadan, in the year 543 of the Hijra (22 January 1149), a certain vizier—or, more properly, wazîr, following the usual Arabic and Persian pronunciation—named ‘Awnoddîn Yahyâ ibn Hobayra was giving a large dinner in Medina, Arabia, to mark the breaking of the fast. Just as the guests were preparing to leave, someone announced that it had begun to rain. The vizier invited them to stay, and the conversation resumed with renewed energy. Eventually the talk turned to religion.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02073

The vizier, a Sunni whose religious convictions were rather simplistic, launched into a violent attack on the Shiites. After all, he said, they were only a minority; and how could a minority possibly be right? May God wipe them from the face of the earth! Now, among the guests was a man to whom the vizier had shown particular respect all evening. This man, whose name we shall never learn and who is to become the hero of our story, listened silently to the vizier’s outburst.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02074

Clearly he was not someone who regarded being in the minority as certain proof of being wrong. At last he spoke. “I should like to contribute to your discussion,” he said, “but only by telling you something I know from my own experience. Otherwise I would rather remain silent.” After a moment’s thought, the vizier replied, “Please, then, tell us what happened to you.”
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02075

The events took place about twenty years before that Ramadan evening, in the year 522/1128, to be exact. The man—who, as the narrative will reveal, was a Christian merchant—begins by describing his homeland, where Muslims form only a small minority. Unfortunately, the geographical clues are very vague. We learn that it is a vast country, requiring two months to cross. There are references to islands and continents, a great city called al-Bahîya (the Beautiful, the Splendid), a common frontier with the Abyssinians and Nubians, and another with the Franks and Byzantines. None of this is enough to locate the country on a map, even if it belongs to the actual geography of our world.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”
passage-en-02076
But that is not, in the end, what matters. What matters is the account of the extraordinary voyage the narrator undertook with his father some twenty years earlier.
II. In the Time of the “Great Occultation”

As usual, they had chartered a ship together with other merchants and put out to sea. What exactly happened next? No one will ever explain it to us. At any rate, they sailed far beyond the time when they should normally have reached their familiar, intended destinations.
